Arctic terns (Sterna paradisaea) begin their lives within calcareous eggs, which are incubated for a period of approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days] when maintained at an internal nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The newly hatched chicks are semi-precocial, emerging with open eyes and a dense covering of downy feathers. Upon hatching, these nestlings exhibit a modest wet weight at birth of 13.1 grams [Wwb = 13.1 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial energetic investment in the yolk-dependent embryo prior to the exotrophic transition. This initial body mass is relatively low compared to some other long-lived seabirds, but it is offset by exceptionally rapid growth rates fueled by intensive biparental provisioning. The altricial nestling period is characterized by a constant parental presence, with one adult remaining at the scrape nest to brood the chick while the other forages, often commuting considerable distances to productive feeding grounds. This brooding behavior is critical for thermoregulation, as the developing chick cannot yet maintain its own body temperature independently.

The nestling chicks experience a phase of accelerated mass gain, transitioning from their neonatal mass to a much larger size before fledging. The maximum recorded adult body mass for this species is approximately 100 grams [Wwi = approximately 100 grams], a figure that represents the ultimate wet weight typical of a healthy, reproductively viable adult. Attaining this adult mass requires the efficient conversion of ingested prey, primarily small fish and crustaceans, into somatic tissue. The time from hatching to the achievement of sustained flight, or fledging, is observed to occur at approximately 22 days after hatching [tx = approximately 22 days after hatching], a duration that falls within the expected range for a bird of this body size and foraging ecology at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This milestone marks the end of the nest-dependent chick phase and heralds a critical period of post-fledging parental care and dietary transition.

The journey toward reproductive capability in the Arctic tern is marked by a clear ontogenetic timeline, with physiological milestones achieved at different rates. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis, is estimated to occur relatively early in the bird's life, at approximately 66 days after hatching [tp = approximately 66 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This early attainment of sexual maturity is somewhat surprising given the species' extended longevity and delayed first reproduction, but it suggests that the reproductive system is prepared well in advance of its actual utilization. The period between fledging and puberty is devoted to honing flight skills, learning to forage efficiently, and undertaking the first long-distance migrations that the species is famous for. During this sub-adult phase, the juvenile bird continues to grow and refine its plumage, gradually acquiring the stark black cap, grey mantle, and deeply forked tail characteristic of the breeding adult. This pre-reproductive juvenile stage is a crucial period for building the body condition necessary to survive the extreme energetic demands of future breeding seasons.

Despite reaching sexual maturity early, Arctic terns defer their first breeding attempt for a considerably longer period. The interval between reaching puberty and undertaking first reproduction is thus a protracted phase of learning and physiological preparation. During this time, the immature bird may return to breeding colonies but remain on the periphery, observing and practicing courtship rituals without participating in nesting. The adaptive significance of this delay is likely linked to the need for a robust body condition, as evidenced by their ultimate adult weight of 100 grams [Wwi = 100 grams], which is required to sustain the metabolic demands of migration and breeding.

Over the course of a single breeding season, the maximum reproductive rate is expressed through a combination of clutch size and frequency; females typically lay one to two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to two eggs per clutch], and usually produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This limited annual output is characteristic of a slow-paced life-history strategy, where each chick represents a significant parental investment in time and resources. The timing of these breeding events is tightly synchronized with the brief Arctic summer, when prey abundance peaks, allowing the adults to capitalize on the seasonal flush of food. The extreme longevity of this species means that even this modest annual reproductive output accumulates over decades, effectively compensating for the delayed onset of first reproduction. This life-history syndrome, combining extended lifespan with deferred maturity and low fecundity, positions the Arctic tern as a classic example of a k-selected species perfectly adapted to a challenging and unpredictable polar environment.
